translations.text: A German poem about King Louis, of pious memory, son of Louis, who was also king.
I know a king; his name is Louis. He gladly serves God, and I know that God rewards him for it.
As a child he lost his father, but he was soon compensated for that: the Lord took him up and became his guardian.
He gave him good qualities, a lordly retinue, and the throne here among the Franks. May he enjoy it for a long time!
Then he soon shared all this with Carloman, his brother: the full measure of joys.
When all that was done, God wished to test him, to see whether he could endure hardships while so young.
He let heathen men sail across the sea to remind the people of the Franks of their sins.
Some were soon lost, and some were chosen. Whoever had lived wickedly before suffered punishment.
Whoever was a thief at that time and came through it took up his fasting [penance], and afterwards he became a good man.
One was a liar, one a robber, one full of lawlessness, and he did penance for it.
The king was far away and the whole kingdom was in disorder. Christ was angry, and sadly the kingdom paid for it.
But God took pity, for he knew all that distress. He commanded Louis to ride there at once: "Louis, my king, help my people!
The Northmen have oppressed them harshly." Then Louis said: "Lord, I will do everything you command, unless death prevents me."
Then he took leave of God, raised the battle standard, and rode into the land of the Franks against the Northmen.
Those who were waiting for him thanked God. They all said: "My lord, we have waited so long for you."
Then Louis the good spoke loudly: "Take heart, comrades, my companions in danger.
God sent me here and gave me his command himself, if it seemed good to you, that I should fight here and not spare myself until I had rescued you.
Now I want all who are loyal to God to follow me. Our life here lasts as long as Christ wills it. If he wills that we depart, he has power over that.
Whoever does God's will here with courage, I will reward him if he comes out of this alive. If he stays there [dies], I will reward his family."
Then he took shield and spear and rode out bravely. He truly wanted to settle accounts with his enemies.
It was not long before he found the Northmen. He gave praise to God, for he saw what he had longed for.
The king rode boldly and sang a holy song, and all of them sang together: "Kyrie eleison."
The song was sung and the battle was begun. Blood shone on cheeks, and the Franks rejoiced in the fight.
No warrior fought there like Louis: swift and bold, as was in his blood.
Some he struck through, some he ran through. With his own hands he served his enemies a bitter drink. Woe to them for ever for their lives!
Praised be the power of God! Louis was victorious. And thanks to all the saints! The victory in battle was his.
Hail then, Louis, blessed king! As ready as he always was, wherever there was need of it, may the Lord keep him in his grace [?].
